title: Tunneling-only access switch: no thermal tail, attoamp off-state
idea: Inverts 'the access device is a thermionic MOSFET': replace it with a vertical heterojunction tunnel-FET (e.g., Ge/Si or GaSb/InAs source pocket) whose OFF current is set by band-to-band tunneling through a closed window rather than the Boltzmann tail. Orient it asymmetrically so the tunnel junction sits on the bitline side and the storage node only sees a wide-gap reverse junction.
why: Attacks the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3): subthreshold component falls toward aA, retention 64 ms -> >10 s, cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% bandwidth tax by >90%; the TFET's low ON current is enough since a cell needs only ~0.5 uA (5 fF x 1 V / 10 ns).

title: Nanomechanical relay access: an air gap is the off-state
idea: Inverts 'the switch must be a semiconductor': each storage capacitor is isolated by an electrostatically actuated NEMS cantilever relay (Ru- or carbon-coated beam over a ~5 nm air gap) that physically breaks contact, so the OFF state is an open circuit and leakage is only through the capacitor dielectric. Bitlines are equalized before contact closes (cold switching) so contacts survive >10^15 cycles.
why: Removes access leakage entirely (fact 3): retention set by dielectric leakage (seconds to hours), refresh energy and bandwidth tax near zero; abrupt relay switching also allows sub-1 V wordlines instead of ~3 V (fact 10).

title: Vacuum-nanogap field-emission access: electrons cross nothing when off
idea: Inverts 'carriers flow through a solid channel': the storage node ends in a sharp nanotip facing the bitline across a sealed ~10 nm vacuum gap; a wordline gate raises the local field above emission threshold for read/write, while below it the exponential Fowler-Nordheim law gives >10^12 on/off with no channel to leak. Gaps are made by sacrificial-layer release plus a wafer-level hermetic ALD seal.
why: Replaces the leakage tail (fact 3) with an off-current far below aA, enabling refresh-free working memory that is also temperature- and radiation-insensitive.

title: Leakage-keeper latch: make the leaks hold the bit, stacked vertically
idea: Inverts 'leakage destroys stored data': build a loadless 4-device latch where the access devices' OFF leakage is engineered ~10x larger than the cross-coupled drivers' leakage, so leakage itself replenishes the high node and the cell is static with no refresh. Stack the four devices in two BEOL tiers (n-type and p-type oxide channels) over CMOS so the footprint approaches a 1T1C cell.
why: Zero refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) and no capacitor (fact 1) at ~6-8F2 footprint via vertical stacking; standby power drops to ~fA per bit.

title: Airlock isolation: a second hold gate that closes only in idle
idea: Inverts 'one access gate must serve both speed and isolation': split the vertical access pillar into a fast low-Vt segment driven by the wordline and an ultra-high-Vt 'hold' segment that is statically on during active periods and driven to about -1.5 V when a bank enters idle/self-refresh. The hold segment switches only on mode changes, so its slowness costs nothing.
why: Idle leakage drops 100-1000x (fact 3), cutting self-refresh power (16-33% of idle) by ~10x while active timing is unchanged; ~1 extra gate layer.

title: Trim each leaky access transistor once, like programming flash
idea: Inverts 'the leakage tail is frozen at fab-out': add a thin nitride trap layer in the access-transistor gate stack; at wafer test retention-profile every cell and apply a one-time hot-carrier program pulse only to the ~0.1% tail cells, raising their Vt by 150-300 mV so their OFF current falls 10-100x. A BIST mode re-trims in the field as cells age.
why: Removes the tail that sets the refresh interval (fact 3): 64 ms -> >=512 ms across the die, ~8x lower refresh energy and bandwidth tax for one extra deposition.

title: Self-healing traps: on-die microheaters anneal leakage defects in the field
idea: Inverts 'aging only makes leakage worse': embed a deuterium-loaded SiN reservoir and a TiN microheater per mat; in scheduled idle windows (data migrated to a spare mat) heat the mat for milliseconds so deuterium diffuses to and passivates the dangling-bond traps that cause trap-assisted junction leakage, resetting the retention tail.
why: Keeps the leakage tail near fresh-wafer levels for life (fact 3), allowing a permanently ~4x longer refresh interval, and partially heals hammer-induced trap generation (fact 9).

title: Let only ones fall: unidirectional-error codes replace frequent refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh must stop every bit from decaying': charge leakage only flips true-cells 1->0 (anti-cells 0->1), so store each row with a Berger-style count code (~10 check bits in opposite-polarity cells) that detects any number of unidirectional errors plus a Z-channel code that corrects them, and stretch refresh until the code margin is nearly consumed.
why: Refresh interval 64 ms -> ~0.5-1 s by tolerating tail-cell decay (fact 3) at ~2-4% storage overhead, recovering most of the 10-20% bandwidth and refresh energy.

title: Data that dies young: refresh-free banks for transient tensors
idea: Inverts 'every byte must be retained until overwritten': the compiler tags each AI tensor with its lifetime (activations and KV segments often live <10 ms), and the memory controller places them in banks whose refresh is masked off, guaranteeing reuse or overwrite within the profiled retention window; only weights and long-lived state sit in refreshed banks.
why: Removes refresh energy and bandwidth loss (fact 3) for most accelerator traffic (worth ~10-20% bandwidth and much of idle power) with only a per-bank refresh-mask command.

title: Refresh that gives energy back: resonant bitline charge recycling
idea: Inverts 'refresh charge is dumped to ground': during refresh bursts, bitline pairs swing through an on-die LC tank (an integrated inductor shared per bank) so the energy of charging bitlines is stored magnetically and returned on the next row, approximating adiabatic charging; random accesses keep conventional sensing.
why: Cuts the ~46 fJ/bit refresh energy (fact 3) by ~3-5x and sidesteps the CV2 floor (fact 10) for the refresh share of DRAM power.

title: Breathing cell plate: park stored charge at the leakage minimum
idea: Inverts 'the cell plate sits at a fixed VDD/2': in idle, ramp the common plate down ~0.3 V so '1' nodes sit lower (shrinking the GIDL and junction fields where the trap-assisted tail lives) while '0' nodes stay just short of forward bias, then ramp back before access; the stored difference is untouched because the plate shifts both states equally.
why: The tail's exponential field dependence (fact 3) gives ~3-10x longer idle retention, cutting self-refresh power proportionally with only a plate-driver change.

title: Gateless rectifier access: ultra-wide-bandgap Schottky diode replaces the transistor
idea: Inverts 'the access device needs a gate': each capacitor reaches its bitline through a vertical Ga2O3 (4.8 eV) Schottky diode and the wordline is the cell plate; to write, raise the plate so the node clamps to the bitline level plus Vf, then drop it ('clamp-and-drop' sets any level), and to read, raise the plate and sense the dumped charge. Reverse leakage in a 4.8 eV material is orders of magnitude below silicon generation current.
why: Removes the 3-terminal transistor, its leakage tail (fact 3) and the 3 V boosted wordline (fact 10); a 2-terminal 4F2 cell stacks without a lateral transistor (fact 2).

title: Battery bit: store data as redox state, not loose charge
idea: Inverts 'a bit is free charge on a capacitor': each cell is a nanoscale solid-state redox couple (e.g., proton-intercalated WO3 against a reservoir) whose open-circuit potential encodes the bit; leakage only slowly shifts state of charge, and a gain transistor whose gate sits on the redox electrode reads it nondestructively.
why: Retention from ms to hours (fact 3) without a high-AR capacitor (fact 1); nondestructive read avoids rewrite energy (fact 8). Risks: 10-100 ns ion kinetics and endurance.

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack: beat 60 mV/decade to close the leak
idea: Inverts 'the Boltzmann 60 mV/dec limit fixes off-leakage for a given wordline swing': add a thin doped-HfO2 negative-capacitance layer to the access gate (as a voltage amplifier only, not storage) to reach ~40 mV/dec, so the same swing yields 10-100x lower Ioff or the same Ioff at ~2 V wordline.
why: Attacks both the leakage tail (fact 3) and the 3 V wordline floor (fact 10): ~10-30x longer retention or ~45% lower wordline CV2.

title: Delete the junction: dielectric-isolated junctionless storage node
idea: Inverts 'the storage node is a doped pn junction': build the access device as an accumulation-mode junctionless transistor in layer-transferred thin silicon on buried oxide, with the capacitor contacting a uniformly doped n+ segment wrapped in dielectric, so there is no depletion region where trap-assisted generation (the dominant tail mechanism) can occur.
why: Cuts the junction/GIDL-driven leakage tail (fact 3) 10-100x, pushing refresh toward seconds, and removes floating-body coupling that aids row hammer (fact 9).

title: Canary cells: deliberately weak cells decide when to refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh is scheduled for the worst cell at the worst temperature': each mat carries a few canary cells built with a 2-3x wider access device (predictably leakier than any real cell) and a continuous-time comparator; a mat is refreshed only when its canary crosses threshold, tracking local temperature, voltage and aging.
why: Most mats retain >=10x longer than spec (fact 3); local triggering cuts average refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~4-8x without per-row profiling tables.

title: Chill the memory, not the room: Peltier-pumped DRAM tier
idea: Inverts 'DRAM runs at whatever temperature the package gives it': a thin-film Bi2Te3 thermoelectric layer between the DRAM stack and the logic die pumps heat out of the DRAM dies to hold them ~25 C below the logic; retention roughly doubles per 10 C, so refresh rate drops ~5x.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth tax (fact 3) fall ~80% and row-hammer thresholds improve (fact 9); makes HBM-on-logic thermally cheaper. Cost is TEC power, partly offset by refresh savings.

title: Atom-thin channel: 2D semiconductor access with no bulk to leak
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor is carved from bulk silicon': grow or transfer monolayer WSe2/MoS2 channels into a BEOL vertical gate-all-around access device; the 0.7 nm body has no junction volume, a 1.6-2 eV gap and full gate control, putting Ioff around 10^-19 A/um and allowing stacking above CMOS.
why: Retention 64 ms -> minutes (fact 3), near refresh-free, and stackable 3D tiers without a lateral silicon transistor (fact 2).

title: Squeeze to switch: strain-gated piezoelectronic access device
idea: Inverts 'a switch is gated by a field in its channel': an AlScN or PMN-PT piezo actuator compresses a SmSe-type piezoresistive channel that undergoes a pressure-driven insulator-to-metal transition; uncompressed, the channel is a true gapped insulator with no subthreshold tail, and actuation needs <0.2 V.
why: Isolation without a subthreshold tail (fact 3) and sub-volt wordlines (fact 10), cutting wordline CV2 ~10x and refresh to near zero.

title: Deliberately non-uniform mats: tall and short capacitors by data lifetime
idea: Inverts 'all cells must be identical': fabricate two retention classes on one die, tall-capacitor long-retention mats (refresh ~1 s) and short-capacitor no-guarantee mats (1-10 ms) that skip the deepest etch, and expose them as separate NUMA tiers so the OS places long-lived pages and transient buffers where each is cheapest.
why: Splits capacitor cost and refresh cost (facts 1, 3): short mats save process steps and area, long mats cut most refresh energy; ~2x better blended cost-energy.

title: Lopsided access transistor: wide-gap storage-side contact kills GIDL
idea: Inverts 'the access transistor is symmetric': replace only the storage-node-side source/drain extension with a thin wide-gap oxide semiconductor contact, so the gate-to-storage overlap, where GIDL band-to-band tunneling dominates, sits in a >3 eV material while the bitline side stays silicon for drive current.
why: BTBT falls exponentially with bandgap, so storage-side GIDL drops ~100x and the tail (fact 3) shrinks enough for ~4-8x longer refresh.

title: Electric double layer storage: ions replace the solid dielectric
idea: Inverts 'the storage dielectric must be a solid insulator': use a nanometre-thin solid polymer or ionogel electrolyte between ion-blocking electrodes so the electric double layer gives ~10-30 uF/cm2 (3-6x high-k ZrO2); blocking electrodes keep DC leakage low and nanoscale thickness keeps the ionic RC short.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1: AR 60-75:1 -> ~15:1) and buys retention margin against access leakage (fact 3); risk is ionic switching speed at ns scale.

title: Pinned storage well: the image-sensor trick buries the bit
idea: Inverts 'the bit must sit on a metal-contacted capacitor': store electrons in a buried n-well under a p+ surface pinning layer (the pinned-photodiode structure from CMOS image sensors, built as a deep vertical well), moved in and out by a transfer gate to a floating-diffusion sense node; the pinning layer keeps interface traps filled with holes so they cannot generate leakage.
why: Pinned wells show orders of magnitude lower dark current than surface or junction nodes, so retention moves from 64 ms toward minutes (fact 3) with no capacitor tower (fact 1); trade-off is a small well and charge-transfer read.

title: Vertical charge-coupled memory: no switch per bit, just moving charge
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs its own access transistor': deposit a 200-layer gate/oxide stack (NAND-style, one hole etch), line each hole with a poly-Si or oxide channel, and clock the layer gates in 3 phases so charge packets march along the hole like a vertical CCD. Each hole holds ~60 bits and one sense/regeneration stage at the top restores packets as they circulate, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: No per-bit transistor, capacitor or litho: cost tracks 3D NAND (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x below DRAM per GB; trade-off is serial access (~us to the far bit, high streaming bandwidth) and transfer-loss risk in poly channels.

title: Dynamic-mode 3D NAND: hold charge in the channel, not the trap
idea: Inverts 'NAND lines can only make nonvolatile flash': operate existing 300-layer 3D NAND strings as capacitorless floating-body cells, injecting holes by GIDL into the poly channel under a selected wordline (neighbors biased as barriers), sensing the Vt shift through the string and refreshing every ~1-10 ms; the trap layer is never programmed, so endurance is unlimited.
why: Taps existing, depreciated NAND fab capacity and flow, ~50-150x cheaper per GB than DRAM; trade-off is ~1-5 us latency, page-granular access and heavy refresh.

title: Volatile flash: a 2 nm tunnel oxide that forgets in seconds
idea: Inverts 'a charge-trap cell that loses data in seconds is a failed flash cell': on standard 3D NAND tools, thin the tunnel oxide to ~1.5-2 nm so programming uses low-field direct tunneling (~3-4 V, ~100 ns) that barely damages the oxide, accept seconds-scale retention, and refresh in large background bursts.
why: Direct tunneling targets 10^12+ endurance for a capacitor-free, transistor-free 3D cell at NAND-like cost (~100x cheaper per GB); trade-off: ~100 ns writes, us page reads, ~1 s refresh.

title: Memory on window glass: multi-tier oxide TFT cells on display lines
idea: Inverts 'memory is made on 300 mm silicon wafers': run 1T1C cells on idle Gen-8.5 to Gen-10.5 LCD/OLED glass lines, stacking 10-20 tiers with KrF-class litho at ~0.3 um and oxide-TFT access whose ultralow leakage lets tiny capacitors skip refresh; dice panels into tiles bonded to a small CMOS controller.
why: Display glass costs ~100-1000x less per area than leading-edge silicon; at 20 tiers and 4F2, ~$0.1-0.4/GB, ~25-100x cheaper; trade-off is ~100 ns-1 us access and lower density per volume.

title: Second life for leaky silicon: refresh-tuned salvage of retention rejects
idea: Inverts 'a die that fails 64 ms retention is scrap': buy fab retention-reject dies and decommissioned server and phone DRAM at scrap prices, profile each chip's retention map on high-throughput testers, and mount them on CXL boards whose controller refreshes at the measured interval (4-8 ms) and remaps the worst rows.
why: Marginal cost is scrap value plus test (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x cheaper per GB, adding supply with no fab and U.S.-sited refurbishment; trade-off is higher refresh energy, ~10-20% bandwidth loss and heterogeneous parts.

title: Drown it in nitrogen: capacitorless tiers holding data for hours
idea: Inverts 'memory must work at room temperature': immerse memory sleds in liquid nitrogen, where subthreshold and generation leakage fall by many decades, so a bare gate-node or floating-body cell in many-tier poly-Si stacks with no capacitor at all retains for minutes to hours; LN2 at ~$0.1/L and cryo-rack designs carry the heat.
why: Deletes the capacitor module (fact 1) and allows cheap many-tier poly stacks with near-zero refresh, claimed ~100x cost/GB at NAND-like layer cost; trade-off is cryo plant energy and logistics.

title: Light is the wordline: photoconductor cells addressed by micro-LED rows
idea: Inverts 'the access device is a transistor on a metal wordline': a blanket wide-gap photoconductor film sits between capacitor dots and metal bitlines, insulating in the dark (retention set by very high dark resistivity), and a row is selected by flashing a stripe of a bonded micro-LED/waveguide array for ~10 ns. No transistors, no wordline drivers, two masks per layer.
why: Removes access transistors and much of the 49% periphery (fact 7) at film-coating cost, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off is optical power per access, 10-100 ns latency and photoconductor persistence.

title: Threshold-switch crossbar capacitors: 64 decks, refreshed constantly
idea: Inverts 'an access device must hold the bit for 64 ms': put a chalcogenide ovonic threshold switch in series with a tiny MIM capacitor at every crossbar node, stack 64 self-aligned decks with two KrF masks each, accept us-to-ms retention set by OTS leakage, and refresh whole decks in parallel from base CMOS.
why: 4F2 per deck with no transistor or EUV, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off is refresh power (~20-40% of total), half-select disturb and OTS drift.

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.
why: Roll-to-roll layers cost ~$1-5/m2 versus ~$10,000/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so even at ~30x lower density it is ~100x cheaper per GB for transient data; trade-off: no long-term storage, ~100 ns-1 us access.

title: Carousel memory: rows stream past a reader, decoders deleted
idea: Inverts 'refresh is a background chore and random access needs decoders': read, regenerate and rewrite every row in a fixed cyclic order every ~1 ms using simple counters (no row/column decoders, no refresh controller), with a small SRAM front buffer catching requested rows as they pass; 1000 parallel carousels cut the wait to ~1 us.
why: Removes most of the 49% periphery (fact 7) and makes refresh the data path, so cells with 1000x worse leakage become usable; with relaxed-cell 3D builds, ~100x cost/GB for latency-tolerant bandwidth tiers.

title: Self-assembled diode dots: block copolymers replace EUV for every cell
idea: Inverts 'lithography must define each access device': coat a PS-b-PDMS block copolymer guided by coarse 193 nm trenches into 10 nm-pitch dot arrays, then convert each dot by sequential infiltration synthesis into a vertical oxide Schottky diode atop a MIM nanocapacitor, mapping out defective dots at test.
why: Zero EUV layers (fact 4) and ~1 mask per tier at 10 nm pitch; with 8 tiers, ~100x lower cost per GB; trade-off is diode leakage forcing ms refresh and DSA defect remapping.

title: Random-wired memory: nanowire mesh with addresses discovered, not designed
idea: Inverts 'every cell has a designed address': spray a random mesh of core-shell nanowires (each a gated-diode storage element) between coarse electrode grids, then let a self-test routine discover which electrode pairs reach a usable cell, store the map in on-chip flash, and address through stochastically doped decoder wires instead of patterned decoders.
why: No overlay or fine litho, so cost tracks coating plus coarse patterning (~100x cheaper per GB claimed), with refresh tuned per discovered cell; trade-off is ~30-60% usable sites and a lookup table.

title: Thousand-times-leakier cells tamed by a refresh engine per tile
idea: Inverts 'access transistors must leak <=13 fA': use the cheapest stackable access devices (unannealed sputtered poly-Si or oxide TFTs leaking ~10 pA) so retention is only ~10-100 us, and put a micro-sense-amp under each 4k-cell tile (CMOS-under-array) that refreshes its own tile continuously without touching global bitlines.
why: Trades refresh energy (~3-5x today) for ~100x lower cost per GB from low-temperature, 2-mask tiers with no deep capacitor; refresh traffic never leaves the tile, so bandwidth is unaffected.

title: Williams tube reborn: MEMS electron beams paint charge on film
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs a transistor': like the 1947 Williams-Kilburn tube, store bits as charge spots on a continuous unpatterned dielectric film, written and read by secondary emission from an array of ~10^4 microfabricated field-emitter beamlets each scanning a ~100 um patch; the beam re-scan doubles as refresh.
why: Cost per bit falls to film coating plus the amortized emitter array, ~100x cheaper per GB claimed; trade-off: us latency, vacuum packaging, emitter lifetime.

title: Predictable decay: compensate unrefreshed analog weights instead of refreshing
idea: Inverts 'decay is an error to prevent': store neural-net weights as 4-6-bit analog charge in simple unrefreshed capacitor cells whose decay is a known exponential, and have the accelerator scale each tile's outputs by exp(+t/tau) using a per-tile timestamp and reference cell, reloading tiles from a NAND copy every few seconds.
why: No refresh circuitry plus 4-6 bits per cheap planar cell on mature nodes gives ~30-100x cheaper per GB for inference weights; trade-off is analog noise and per-cell tau spread.

title: Anodized aluminum capacitor forest: 1000:1 aspect ratio for free
idea: Inverts 'high-aspect-ratio capacitors need costly etch': anodize thick aluminum to self-organize vertical pores at ~40-60 nm pitch and ~1000:1 aspect ratio, then ALD-line them with TiN/ZrO2/TiN, giving tens of fF per cell so that cheap, leaky TFT access devices still retain for seconds.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) without deep RIE or EUV and lets low-cost leaky access meet retention (fact 3); stacked with TFT tiers, claimed ~100x cost/GB; trade-off is larger pitch and slower bitline sensing.

title: Colors pick the layer: wavelength-addressed 3D stacks without staircases
idea: Inverts 'each 3D tier needs its own wired wordline contact': give each tier a photoconductive access element made of quantum dots tuned to a distinct absorption band (16 tiers, 16 wavelengths) and run a light pipe per column, so choosing the wavelength selects the tier and all tiers share their electrical lines with no staircase or tier-specific masks.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier wiring (fact 2), allowing 16-64 tiers at single-tier mask count, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: optical crosstalk, us-class access, dot stability.

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.
why: Two-terminal low-mask crossbar with refresh-free retention, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: heater energy per row access, thermal crosstalk, ~100 ns cycle.

title: Woven memory: crossbar cells where drawn fibers cross in a textile
idea: Inverts 'memory is lithographed on a flat wafer': thermally draw multimaterial fibers (metal core with Schottky-diode shell, or metal core with dielectric shell) down to ~1 um by the kilometre, then weave or align-lay them orthogonally so every crossing is a diode-capacitor cell, and stack woven sheets into blocks.
why: Fiber drawing makes km of device per hour at material cost, so a 100-layer block reaches ~$0.1/GB-class (~100x cheaper); trade-off: low areal density, slow high-capacitance lines, contact variability.

title: Virtual cells: unpatterned film where fields, not etches, isolate bits
idea: Inverts 'each access transistor is a patterned island': deposit a blanket, unetched oxide-semiconductor film over crossing gate grids, and bias a 'fence' grid negative so it depletes the film around every crossing, electrostatically forming isolated storage pockets and access channels; each tier needs only metal-line masks, no active-area or channel etch.
why: Cuts per-tier masks 2-3x and removes etched channel edges that feed the leakage tail (fact 3); at 32+ tiers, claimed ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: fence bias power, isolation set by film quality.

title: Crested-barrier capacitor: the capacitor is its own access switch
idea: Inverts 'storage and switch are separate devices': each crossbar node is a floating metal nanolayer between two crested tunnel barriers (e.g., nitride/AlN/nitride trilayers) whose peak collapses at high field, giving ~10^12 current change between the ~3 V write and ~1 V hold; charge on the floating layer is the bit, written in ns by tunneling and read capacitively, from one blanket deposition per deck.
why: No transistor, no capacitor tower, one deposition per deck in 4F2 crossbar stacks, ~100x cheaper per GB; crested barriers reduce oxide stress, aiming at 10^12+ endurance; trade-off: write energy and unproven endurance.

title: One global clock restores every cell: gated-diode charge-pump bistables
idea: Inverts 'refresh is done row by row by sense amps': each cell is a gated diode (large capacitance when inverted, small when depleted) tied to a shared plate clock and a diode to the supply; a stored '1' couples the clock strongly and is topped up each cycle while a '0' couples weakly and stays below the diode threshold, so one global clock refreshes billions of cells at once.
why: Lets cheap leaky TFT or poly cells work with no row refresh, sense-amp refresh path or refresh controller (fact 7), ~2 devices per cell in low-mask tiers, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: continuous clock power and margin between stable points.

title: Single-electron grains: revive room-temperature polysilicon percolation memory
idea: Inverts 'a bit needs ~30,000 electrons behind a switch': use an ultrathin (~3 nm) polysilicon strip whose natural grains form a percolation channel, where trapping a few electrons on one grain via Coulomb blockade shifts conduction measurably (Yano-type cell); retention is set by the blockade barrier, not a transistor off-state, and strips can be self-aligned sidewalls without fine litho.
why: ~10^11-10^12 bits/cm2 from simple poly deposition and minimal masks, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: large variability needing heavy ECC and mapping, ms-s retention with refresh, temperature sensitivity.
